newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam diplomat warns of risk to open-door policy.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam diplomat warns of risk to open-door policy.

text.p: A former senior Vietnamese diplomat warned on Saturday that Hanoi's decade-old open-door policy was facing difficulties from forces within the government opposed to free trade.
Nguyen Co Thach told Reuters that some delegates at the current National Assembly session were pushing for measures aimed at slowing trade liberalisation.

"I think it (the open-door policy) will have more progress," he said. "...But there are still some difficulties. For instance in this conference there's somebody who would like to have production to substitute imports."
Thach, Vietnam's foreign minister between 1980 and 1991, was speaking during a break in Saturday's assembly session.
He did not identify the opponents of liberalisation.

Government officials have expressed concern in recent months over a soaring trade deficit, which reached nearly $3.54 billion in the period between January 1 and September 10 compared with $2.3 billion for all of last year.
A General Statistics Office report, released earlier this month, said the deficit was not yet having an impact on the economy but added it was "much higher than should be allowed".
The report called for increased efforts to tackle smuggling and for restrictions on the import of goods, such as cement, which are produced in-country.

Vietnam has committed itself to lower trade tariffs with fellow members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) over the next few years. Hanoi has also applied for membership in the World Trade Organisation.
But Western economists say vested interests are preventing Hanoi from demonstrating real commitment to free trade.
A recent report compiled by Swedish analysts said owners of state-owned enterprises and foreign multinationals which benefit from protectionism were opposing liberalisation.
A revised foreign investment law, which is expected to be approved by the current National Assembly, is also set to exclude overseas firms from participating in certain sectors of the economy.
Thach did not refer to the new law, but said that despite growing opposition, the prevailing mood was still in favour of reforms.
"Now the main current is for exportation, and you see in the text (of government reports) there is no mention of import substitution," he said. "But some still raise this question."
